Key issues, including whether the state’s “home rule” is the cause of its segregated school system and how the state failed to address racial disparities, remained unresolved as well.

items.title: Three studies in a row show teeny-tiny or zero academic gains from school cellphone bans
items.summary:
Since 2023, cellphone use during the school day has been banned or restricted in at least 40 states and the District of Columbia, in the hope that reducing digital distractions would help students focus on their lessons.

So how’s it working?

Last week researchers at Harvard University released the third major study of cellphone limits in U.S. schools and, like the two before it, it found remarkably little academic benefit. Media reports trumpeted the study’s findings of gains in student achievement as evidence of real progress . But read the fine print: Students’ combined math and reading scores, as measured by MAP tests, rose by only an extra 0.0087 of a standard deviation.

Readers, I try to avoid talking about abstract statistical units, but in this case, they’re important because they show just how teeny-tiny the academic gains were. The estimated improvement is less than one-hundredth of a standard deviation, a very small shift in student performance. In graduate school, I was taught that even an improvement of one-tenth of a standard deviation — more than 10 times the size of this effect — is quite small.

But the Harvard researchers translated that 0.0087 improvement into one to two weeks of additional learning a year. They characterized the gains as “modest” and said they could add up over time and help students recover half of the learning losses that accumulated between 2013 and 2020, before student performance took a steeper nosedive during the pandemic.

The tiny gain was found after comparing student achievement in schools where students had to put their…
items.t: Three studies in a row show teeny-tiny or zero academic gains from school cellphone bans

items.title: OPINION: It’s time to put curiosity, creativity and critical thinking first in the early learning years
items.summary:
Early education is often judged by how quickly children master the 3 Rs: reading, writing and arithmetic. Those skills are essential, but not sufficient.

Children also need the 3 Cs: curiosity, creativity and critical thinking.

We often treat the 3 Cs as “nice-to-haves” after children master reading, writing and arithmetic. But that gets the sequence backward.

Curiosity draws a child toward a book. Creativity links ideas in new ways as the child reads. Critical thinking helps the child assess whether those ideas fit together.

The 3 Cs are not a reward for finishing the academic work. Instead, they drive learning and make it stick.

Few educators would argue that the 3 Cs are unimportant. The problem is that we have organized early education around the 3 Rs . Further, our approach to these basic skills often reflects a predominantly academic style of teaching in the early years, with a proliferation of scripted curricula, worksheets, drills and questions with a single expected answer. I propose weaving the 3 Cs into early learning at school and at home through rich, back-and-forth conversations, open-ended questions and guided play.

Related: Young children have unique needs and providing the right care can be a challenge. Our free early childhood education newsletter tracks the issues. 

In the early years, children learn what thinking feels like and discover with pride and excitement that they can generate their own ideas. Consider two pre-K classrooms:

In the first, a teacher asks, “Which block tower is taller?” An eager child gives the right answer, and the teacher…
items.t: OPINION: It’s time to put curiosity, creativity and critical thinking first in the early learning years

items.title: The Guardian view on Ofsted: its damaged relationship with schools in England needs fixing | Editorial
items.summary:
The government, as well as the inspectorate, must take responsibility for reforms that have not worked out

The inspection and rating of schools is, by definition, a fraught process. There are few things that parents care more about than the education of their children. For teachers and headteachers, it is stressful and exposing to have their work judged. At a time when shrinking school rolls are leading to closures, the stakes are even higher. An unpopular school with empty places is far more likely to be asked to merge, or close, than one that is sought after by parents.

Policymakers have a tough job to strike a balance between the undeniable pressure that the watchdog places on schools in England and the benefits to families of information to aid their choices. But the coroner’s verdict on the death of Ruth Perry, a headteacher who took her own life in 2023, tipped the balance away from a system that relied too heavily on one-word judgments. On a late spring day in 1995, Mayor Richard M. Daley called his chief budget and finance director, Paul Vallas, into his City Hall office.

Republican lawmakers, responding to a prolonged financial and governance crisis in Chicago Public Schools, were going to hand control of the district to the mayor. Daley told the 42-year-old Vallas, a hard-charging number-cruncher lacking management experience in public education, that he wanted him to be the district’s first CEO.

“He didn’t really ask me,” Vallas said. “I was eager to do it.”

Thus began three decades of mayoral governance that would take Chicago Public Schools from being labeled as the worst in the nation to a national leader of education reform to a district struggling with enrollment declines. It gave Chicago’s mayor authority to appoint everyone on the Chicago Board of Education, and effectively final say over major decisions that affected schools.

Denise Wilson decided to become a Memphis teacher 10 years ago while working at a local Wendy’s.

“I had a lot of teenagers that worked for me that were having trouble counting money,” she said. “So I started teaching them how, and they were like, ‘You make it so easy. You should be a teacher.’”

She took that advice to heart, joining Teach For America and later taking a first grade position at Winchester Elementary in Whitehaven. Wilson has been there for a decade, moving up to fifth grade, but she hasn’t lost her knack for food service.

In January 2025, Wilson helped create a food pantry at Winchester that sent 30 students home each week with grocery boxes containing enough food to feed their families. The pantry’s reach has grown since then, now serving roughly three-quarters of Winchester’s student population, she told Chalkbeat.

“Last I counted, it was 252 students who every Friday leave the building with a bag of non-perishable, easy to fix food, so they can have food over the weekend,” Wilson said. Families also get a refrigerated bag with milk and eggs, and a freezer bag with various types of meat.…
items.t: Last year, this Memphis teacher started a school food pantry. It now serves over 250 students.

items.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
From inheritance to nepotism in the workplace, social inequality is now a daily experience for many young people

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.title: Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult | Lola Okolosie
items.summary:
I welcome Alan Milburn’s call for schools to focus more on students’ potential beyond exams. Yet I must ask: where is the money?

At 16, life should feel like a path leading to endless opportunities. That is at least the carrot dangled in front of young people to motivate them through the gruelling years of exam preparation. “Your life starts now,” their teachers all but tell them. And though for the vast majority that is true, there is a cohort who are forced to accept that the bright futures they were promised are beyond their reach. They are the nearly one million young people aged between 16 and 24 who are not in education, employment or training (Neets).

Alan Milburn’s second report on the nation’s Neets places schools at the heart of the solution. It proposes that schools should be judged not only on grades but also whether pupils continue their post-16 journey into further education or work. Technical education, it also argues, must be regarded with the same gravitas as the academic. Most people working in education won’t argue with this rationale. As ever, the sticking point is how it is to be funded.

Lola Okolosie is an English teacher and writer

items.t: Teachers want to prepare pupils for post-16 life. This is why it’s so difficult | Lola Okolosie

items.title: OPINION: For a well-prepared workforce, schools must rethink the kinds of skills that will be useful in a changing economy
items.summary:
For years, the debate about artificial intelligence and jobs has understandably focused on which workers machines will replace. People are worried about job security, and employers are seeking efficiencies. 

Yet as AI-supported tasks and outputs become increasingly commonplace in virtually every workplace, the conversation is shifting. It’s becoming clear that the best way for today’s K-12 students to “AI-proof” themselves is to lean into the human skills that AI can’t replicate.

Hiring data backs this up. A recent report found that when employers add duties to the jobs most exposed to AI, those new responsibilities are more than twice as likely to call for human strengths like empathy, judgment and creativity. 

The shift is sharpest at the entry level. The same report found that junior positions with the highest AI exposure are seven times more likely than the least exposed ones to require skills like leadership and strategic thinking, which employers have traditionally sought in more experienced workers.

The message is not that automation poses no risk, or that fears of job loss are unfounded. Rather, it is that the costs of neglecting skills such as communication and collaboration are harder to ignore and that failure to develop durable skills heightens the risk.

items.title: Sold a story: It’s up to us

This podcast, Sold a Story, was produced by APM Reports and reprinted with permission. 

Sold a Story is an investigative podcast about how kids learn — what works in the classroom, the science behind those insights and why that research often doesn’t make it into schools. The guidance directs schools and districts not to inspect a student’s body, request photographs of a student’s body, ask for DNA or genetic testing, require physical exams to determine sex, require affidavits related to a student’s reproductive system, or question students about intimate medical information.

The Colorado Department of Education released the 6-page guidance document to schools and districts Wednesday, about six weeks before Proposition 134 is set to take effect on Jan. 1.

The guidance frees schools from the controversial task of verifying students’ sex when they join boys or girls sports teams, but it could anger backers of the ballot measure, which passed 52-48%. items.title: New state dashboard reveals Colorado young people need more help connecting to college and careers
items.summary:
On Monday, Gov. Jared Polis unveiled a new data dashboard focused on young people’s career readiness, civic experiences, and personal well-being. It’s an initiative he pushed for during his time as chair of the National Governors Association.

The new scorecard shows the state scored a 21.14 out of 30 this year in the postsecondary and workforce category. When compared to data compiled from 2019, this is just a .17 increase. The tool tracks whether 18- to 24-year-olds have graduated with work experience or credentials, enrolled in postsecondary learning programs or are unemployed.

Polis has leaned into recent U.S. News and World Report rankings that say Colorado is ranked No. 1 in education, including when he announced the state’s Let’s Get Ready tool. But Polis’ own data reveals more needs to be done to help Colorado’s young people connect to the workforce, career training, or college.

Polis said the tool will help state officials identify areas that need more focus. He will leave office in January, and his administration has said the tool is fully customizable for the next governor to tweak.
